Description: A large sacrificial altar of cut calcareous sandstone ashlars with chiselled horns on four corners, reconstructed to over 5 feet high (about 3 cubits, matching Exodus 27:1–2). Its stones were found in 1973 by Yohanan Aharoni at Tel Beersheba, reused in a storehouse wall in secondary use. The original is now in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem, and a reconstructed replica stands at the Tel Beersheba national park entrance. Burn marks show sacrifices were performed on it.
Interpretations: Two debates must be stated. First, when it was dismantled: Aharoni's 1973 press release linked the dismantling to Hezekiah's reform (2 Kings 18:1–4), while Yigael Yadin suggested it could be the altar of 2 Kings 23:8 destroyed by Josiah, and pottery from the dismantling layer has been dated 640–620 BCE, which points toward Josiah; most scholars now favour Hezekiah, but the question is not settled. Second, whom it served: its finely cut ashlars contrast with the unhewn stones of the Arad altar and with Deuteronomy 27:6's whole-stone rule, and one source suggests it may have served a pagan cult under kings such as Ahaz rather than Yahweh worship. Amos denounces worship at Beersheba (Amos 8:14).
BiblicalSignificance: It is the largest horned altar found in Israel and matches the tabernacle altar's dimensions in Exodus, while its deliberate dismantling illustrates the cultic reforms that centralised worship in Jerusalem.
CurrentLocation: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (original); replica at Tel Beersheba
